\chapter{Being Your Years}
\label{ch:ge-alter}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask how old somebody is and say my own age in German, using the verb German insists on for it.}

This material was the second half of the hand-written haben chapter, and it could not stay there: ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt needs ich bin, and Wie alt bist du? needs du bist — both of which the chapter on sein teaches. It sits here instead, immediately after that chapter, where every word it needs is already owned, and it closes the haben chapter's open question by showing the one everyday sentence where German refuses that verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[alt]{alt — \textquotedblleft{}old\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C14-alt}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{ich bin müde}. Here is a second adjective to put in the same slot, and it opens a sentence you will be asked for constantly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: alt}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{alt} — \textquotedblleft{}old.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

One syllable. It behaves exactly as \emph{müde} did: after \emph{sein} an adjective takes no ending at all, so \emph{ich bin alt} needs nothing added.

It is the same word as English \textbf{old}, and you can nearly hear it — German kept the \emph{a} where English rounded it.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-a} — short and clipped, the \emph{a} of English \emph{hat}.
  \item \texttt{d-t-final} — the \emph{-lt} closes crisply, both consonants sounded.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}alt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}alt, old\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the verb — \textquotedblleft{}ich bin alt\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}ich bin müde\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}alt, alt — old.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}old.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Alt}.) Does it take an ending after \emph{bin}? (\textbf{No}.) Which English word is it? (\emph{\textbf{Old}}.) Next: the noun that goes with it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[das Jahr]{das Jahr — \textquotedblleft{}the year\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C14-jahr}



\begin{quote}
A noun you have already met inside a longer word, now on its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: das Jahr}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{das Jahr} — \textquotedblleft{}the year.\textquotedblright{} Plural: \textbf{die Jahre}.
\end{quote}

Capitalised, because it is a noun and German capitalises all of them. The plural adds \emph{-e} and takes \emph{die}, as plurals do.

You have seen it before without being told: \emph{die \textbf{Jahres}zeiten}, the seasons, is \textquotedblleft{}the year's times.\textquotedblright{} The year was sitting inside that word the whole time.

The age sentence wants the plural — you are so many \emph{Jahre} old — so it is \emph{Jahre} that will do the work from here.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{j-as-y} — German \emph{j} is the \emph{y} of English \emph{yes}. So \emph{Jahr} opens like \emph{year}, not like \emph{jar}.
  \item \texttt{h-silent-lengthening} — that \emph{h} is not pronounced. It is the silent lengthening \emph{h} you met inside \emph{gehen}, and \emph{Jahr} was named there as one of the three words that hide it, beside \emph{sehr} and \emph{Ihnen}. Here it is.
  \item \texttt{long-a} — so the vowel runs long: \emph{YAAR}. Say it beside English \emph{year} and the two are almost the same noise.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}das Jahr\textquotedblright{} — \emph{j} as \emph{y}, \emph{h} silent, \emph{a} long
  \item singular and plural — \textquotedblleft{}das Jahr, die Jahre\textquotedblright{}
  \item where you had already met it — \textquotedblleft{}die Jahreszeiten\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}das Jahr, die Jahre.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the year.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Das Jahr}.) And the plural. (\textbf{Die Jahre}.) How is the \emph{J} sounded? (\textbf{Like English \emph{y}}.) What is the \emph{h} doing? (\textbf{Lengthening the vowel} — it is not pronounced.) Which longer word has \emph{Jahr} inside? (\emph{\textbf{Jahreszeiten}}.) Next: where \emph{Jahr} and \emph{alt} both come from.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Jahr und alt]{Jahr and alt, taken apart}

\label{lesson:GE-C14-jahr-alt}



\begin{quote}
Two words, both inherited rather than borrowed, and one of them has a Latin cousin you would never guess.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{from} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Jahr} & Germanic *\emph{jēra} & \textbf{year} \\
\textbf{alt} & Germanic *\emph{aldaz} & \textbf{old} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Neither line passes through Latin, which is worth noticing in a chapter about age: German borrowed its \textbf{month} names wholesale from Latin, and kept its own words for the year and for being old.

Now the cousin. The root behind *\emph{aldaz} also went into Latin, as \emph{alere} — \textquotedblleft{}to \textbf{nourish}, to grow.\textquotedblright{} From \emph{alere} English took \textbf{adult}, which is literally \textquotedblleft{}grown up.\textquotedblright{}

So \emph{alt} and \emph{adult} are the same idea taken down two roads: something that has been fed and has grown. Ageing as growth rather than as decay, which is a kinder picture than English usually admits to.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two twins — \textquotedblleft{}Jahr, year; alt, old\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Latin cousin — \textquotedblleft{}alt, alere, adult\textquotedblright{}
  \item what the root meant — \textquotedblleft{}to nourish, to grow\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Jahr, year. Alt, old.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English word is \emph{Jahr}? (\emph{\textbf{Year}}.) And \emph{alt}? (\emph{\textbf{Old}}.) Which English word comes from \emph{alt}'s Latin cousin? (\emph{\textbf{Adult}}.) What did that cousin mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{To nourish, to grow}.\textquotedblright{}) Next: the question you will be asked with these two words.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Wie alt bist du?]{Wie alt bist du?}

\label{lesson:GE-C14-wie-alt-bist-du}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{wie}, you have \emph{alt}, and you have \emph{du bist}. That is the whole question.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Wie alt bist du?}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Wie alt bist du?} — \textquotedblleft{}How old are you?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Four words, and every one of them is already yours. Read it against the English and nothing has moved: \emph{how} — \emph{old} — \emph{are} — \emph{you}.

That is not a coincidence to be grateful for; it is inheritance. Neither language borrowed this question from the other. They have been asking it the same way since before either was called German or English.

The verb sits second, as it does in every German statement and question with a question word in front — \emph{Wie} first, \emph{bist} second, and the rest behind.

To someone you would address formally, it is \emph{Wie alt sind Sie?} — the same question with the polite form of the verb.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Wie alt bist du?\textquotedblright{}
  \item it against the English — \textquotedblleft{}how old are you; wie alt bist du\textquotedblright{}
  \item the formal one — \textquotedblleft{}Wie alt sind Sie?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Wie alt bist du?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask how old someone is, informally. (\textbf{Wie alt bist du?}) And formally. (\textbf{Wie alt sind Sie?}) Which word sits second? (\emph{\textbf{Bist}}.) How many of the four words were new? (\textbf{None}.) Next: how to answer it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt]{ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt}

\label{lesson:GE-C14-alter}



\begin{quote}
The answer, and it is as English as the question was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt.} — \textquotedblleft{}I am twenty years old.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Word for word, that is the English sentence: \emph{I} — \emph{am} — \emph{twenty} — \emph{years} — \emph{old}. Put any number you own in the middle and the sentence is yours.

And German shortens it the same way English does. \emph{Ich bin zwanzig} is complete and ordinary, exactly as \textquotedblleft{}I'm twenty\textquotedblright{} is — the \emph{Jahre alt} can go, and in speech usually does.

Notice which verb is doing the work: \emph{bin}. Not \emph{habe}. Hold on to that, because it is the whole point of the next lesson.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the short form — \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin zwanzig.\textquotedblright{}
  \item your own age, in both lengths
  \item the question and the answer together
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I am twenty years old.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt}.) Shorten it. (\textbf{Ich bin zwanzig}.) Which verb does it use? (\emph{\textbf{Bin}}.) Which does it \textbf{not} use? (\emph{\textbf{Habe}}.) Next: why that choice puts German and English on one side and every Romance language on the other.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sein, nicht haben]{sein, not haben}

\label{lesson:GE-C14-alter-sein-haben}



\begin{quote}
You spent a whole chapter on \emph{haben}. Here is the everyday sentence where German refuses to let you use it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: you ARE your years}]
\begin{quote}
German states age with \textbf{sein}, never with \emph{haben}.
\end{quote}

*\emph{Ich habe zwanzig Jahre} is not German. It is not a clumsy way of putting it; it is not a sentence.

Look what happens when you line the languages up:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{how age works} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{German} & \emph{ich \textbf{bin} … Jahre alt} & I \textbf{am} … \\
\textbf{English} & \emph{I \textbf{am} twenty} & I \textbf{am} … \\
French & \emph{j'\textbf{ai} vingt ans} & I \textbf{have} … \\
Spanish & \emph{t\textbf{engo} veinte años} & I \textbf{have} … \\
Italian & \emph{h\textbf{o} venti anni} & I \textbf{have} … \\
Portuguese & \emph{t\textbf{enho} vinte anos} & I \textbf{have} … \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two on one side, four on the other, and the line falls exactly where the families do.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Romance has its years; Germanic is its years.} Age as something you carry against age as something you are — two pictures of the same fact, and each family committed to one of them long ago.

What makes German's choice worth pointing at is that German did \emph{not} hold the Latin line out generally. Its month names are Latin borrowings wholesale; \emph{Januar}, \emph{Februar} and the rest came in and stayed. But on this sentence, said several times a week for a lifetime, German kept its own logic.

The words a language uses most are the ones it is least willing to trade — which is the same force that keeps its commonest verbs irregular.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the rule — \textquotedblleft{}age takes sein, not haben\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two sides — \textquotedblleft{}ich bin zwanzig; j'ai vingt ans\textquotedblright{}
  \item the picture — \textquotedblleft{}Romance has its years, Germanic is its years\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt — bin, not habe.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb does German use for age? (\emph{\textbf{Sein}}.) Which does French use? (\emph{\textbf{Avoir}} — \textquotedblleft{}to have\textquotedblright{}.) Which two languages sit together here? (\textbf{German and English}.) Did German borrow its month names from Latin? (\textbf{Yes} — which is what makes keeping this sentence its own worth noticing.) Next: the chapter said through.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — asking and answering an age}

\label{lesson:GE-C14-alter-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. One question, one answer, and one thing to keep hearing: which verb carries it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Wie alt bist du?} & How old are you? \\
\emph{Zwanzig Jahre alt. Und du?} & Twenty years old. And you? \\
\emph{Ich bin achtzehn.} & I am eighteen. \\
\emph{Und du bist müde.} & And you are tired. \\
\emph{Aber nicht alt!} & But not old! \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every line runs on the same verb, and two of them drop it the way speech does — \emph{zwanzig Jahre alt} answers the question on its own. Nothing here needs \emph{haben}, and the last two lines put \emph{müde} and \emph{alt} side by side in the slot they share.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the question, then your own answer
  \item the answer short, then long
  \item the two sides — \textquotedblleft{}ich bin zwanzig; j'ai vingt ans\textquotedblright{}
  \item the twins — \textquotedblleft{}Jahr, year; alt, old; alt, adult\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Wie alt bist du? Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask someone's age. (\textbf{Wie alt bist du?}) Answer with your own, both long and short. Which verb does German use, and which does it refuse? (\emph{\textbf{Sein}}; \textbf{not} \emph{haben}.) Which English word shares a root with \emph{alt}? (\emph{\textbf{Adult}}.) Which four languages say \textquotedblleft{}I have twenty years\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
